title: Privacy Complete Guide
subtitle: Master Blockchain Privacy from Fundamentals to Advanced Techniques

intro.title: Introduction to Blockchain Privacy
intro.content:
Privacy is a fundamental human right, yet blockchain technology presents a paradox: while offering financial sovereignty and censorship resistance, most blockchains are completely transparent. Every transaction, wallet balance, and trading pattern is publicly visible forever.

This transparency creates serious risks. When you receive payment in ETH, the sender can see your entire transaction history and current holdings. When you donate to a charity, everyone knows how much you gave. When you trade on a DEX, MEV bots and competitors can track your strategies. This guide explores how blockchain privacy works, why it matters, and how to protect yourself.

Unlike traditional finance where privacy is the default, blockchain requires active measures to maintain financial confidentiality. Through zero-knowledge proofs, stealth addresses, mixers, and encrypted smart contracts, a new generation of privacy tools is making it possible to transact privately while maintaining the benefits of blockchain technology.

why_privacy.title: Why Privacy Matters on Blockchain
why_privacy.content: Privacy isn't about hiding illegal activity—it's about protecting legitimate financial information from unwanted surveillance, competitors, criminals, and oppressive regimes.

blockchain_transparency.title: The Blockchain Transparency Problem
blockchain_transparency.content:
Public blockchains like Ethereum and Bitcoin record every transaction permanently on a transparent ledger. Anyone can view:

  • All your transactions: Every payment, swap, NFT purchase, contract interaction
  • Complete balance history: How much you held at any point in time
  • Transaction patterns: When you're active, what protocols you use, who you interact with
  • Token holdings: Your entire portfolio across all tokens and NFTs
  • DeFi positions: Your lending, borrowing, liquidity providing activities

Real example: In 2020, a victim of a $5 wrench attack (physical theft through violence) had their entire crypto holdings stolen because thieves could see their Ethereum address balance before targeting them. Total loss: over $1 million.

Once someone connects your real-world identity to your wallet address—through an exchange withdrawal, ENS name, social media post, or even receiving payment—your entire financial history becomes visible. This creates risks that don't exist in traditional finance.

financial_privacy.title: Financial Privacy Rights
financial_privacy.content:
In traditional finance, only you and your bank can see your account balance and transactions. This privacy protects:

  • Personal safety: Criminals can't see how much money you have
  • Business strategy: Competitors can't track your operations and suppliers
  • Salary confidentiality: Employers can't see your other income sources
  • Donation privacy: Political or charitable giving remains personal
  • Spending habits: Your purchases aren't public knowledge

Businesses absolutely need privacy: Imagine if Starbucks accepted Ethereum payments and competitors could see their exact revenue, supplier payments, cash reserves, and business strategy in real-time. This is why major companies haven't widely adopted transparent blockchain payments.

Individual needs: You shouldn't have to choose between using blockchain technology and revealing your entire financial life. Privacy is about normalcy, not criminality.

real_world_risks.title: Real-World Privacy Risks
real_world_risks.content:
Blockchain transparency creates concrete dangers that have harmed real users:

1. Physical security threats:

  • $5 wrench attacks targeting known crypto holders
  • Home invasions after address balances become public
  • Kidnapping attempts targeting wealthy wallet owners
  • Real case: Multiple Bitcoin holders attacked after blockchain analysis revealed holdings

2. Financial exploitation:

  • MEV bots sandwiching your trades after seeing pending transactions
  • Competitors copying successful trading strategies
  • Price manipulation when large holders' intentions become visible
  • Phishing campaigns targeting users of specific protocols

3. Discrimination and censorship:

  • Exchanges blacklisting addresses based on transaction history
  • Services refusing users who interacted with certain protocols
  • Financial censorship based on political donations or associations
  • Employers discriminating based on DeFi activities

4. Surveillance and control:

  • Authoritarian governments tracking dissidents' crypto donations
  • Mass surveillance of financial activities without warrants
  • Creating permanent records of all financial behavior
  • Social credit systems based on blockchain activity

The fundamental issue: In traditional finance, privacy is the default and transparency requires justification (like audits or court orders). In blockchain, it's reversed—total transparency is default and privacy requires technical expertise. This imbalance needs correction.

privacy_technologies.title: Core Privacy Technologies
privacy_technologies.content: Modern blockchain privacy relies on cryptographic innovations that allow verification without revealing information. These technologies range from proven solutions used for years to cutting-edge research being deployed today.

zero_knowledge_proofs.title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs)
zero_knowledge_proofs.content:
Zero-knowledge proofs are the foundation of modern blockchain privacy. They allow you to prove something is true without revealing why it's true.

Simple analogy: Imagine proving you're over 21 without revealing your exact birthdate. A ZKP lets you show 'I am over 21' is true without exposing any other information.

How ZKPs work in blockchain:

  1. You want to send 10 ETH privately
  2. You create a cryptographic proof that you own 10 ETH and want to transfer it
  3. The blockchain verifies the proof mathematically
  4. Transaction executes without revealing sender, recipient, or amount

Types of ZKPs:

zk-SNARKs (Zero-Knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge):

  • Very small proof size (~200 bytes)
  • Fast verification (milliseconds)
  • Used by Zcash, Railgun, Aztec
  • Require trusted setup ceremony (potential vulnerability if setup is compromised)
  • Best for: Private transactions and DeFi

zk-STARKs (Zero-Knowledge Scalable Transparent Arguments of Knowledge):

  • Larger proof size (~100KB)
  • No trusted setup needed (more secure)
  • Resistant to quantum computers
  • Used by StarkNet, Polygon Miden
  • Best for: Scaling and long-term security

Real-world privacy example - Zcash:
Zcash pioneered zk-SNARKs for blockchain privacy in 2016. A shielded Zcash transaction reveals nothing:
- Sender address: Hidden
- Recipient address: Hidden
- Amount: Hidden
- Transaction still verifiably valid through ZKP

Over $30 billion in shielded transactions have been processed, proving the technology works at scale.

Advanced applications beyond payments:

  • Private DeFi: Railgun lets you use Uniswap, Aave, and other DeFi protocols while keeping balances and actions private
  • Private voting: Prove you're eligible to vote and submit your vote without revealing your choice
  • Private authentication: Prove you own 100 ETH or an NFT without revealing your address
  • Compliance without disclosure: Prove funds aren't from sanctioned sources without revealing transaction history

The future of ZKPs: As proof generation gets faster and cheaper, ZKPs will enable mainstream privacy-preserving applications that are indistinguishable from normal blockchain use in terms of UX and cost.

mixers.title: Mixers and Privacy Pools
mixers.content:
Mixers (also called tumblers) break the connection between sender and recipient by pooling funds from multiple users and redistributing them.

How traditional mixers work:

  1. Multiple users deposit the same amount (e.g., 1 ETH each) into a pool
  2. Deposits are mixed together in a smart contract
  3. Users can later withdraw to a fresh address
  4. Observers can't tell which deposit corresponds to which withdrawal

Example - Tornado Cash (before sanctions):

  • Over $7 billion in volume processed (2019-2022)
  • Fixed denomination pools: 0.1, 1, 10, 100 ETH
  • Used zk-SNARKs to prove you deposited without revealing which deposit
  • Anonymity set size: thousands of users per pool

How anonymity sets work:
If 1,000 people deposited 1 ETH and you withdraw, observers know you're one of those 1,000 but can't tell which. The larger the anonymity set, the stronger the privacy. For 1,000 users, you have 1-in-1,000 plausible deniability.

The Tornado Cash controversy:
In August 2022, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned Tornado Cash, claiming it facilitated money laundering. This raised fundamental questions:
- Is privacy technology illegal, or just certain uses of it?
- Can code be sanctioned like a person or entity?
- Where's the line between privacy rights and preventing crime?

The sanctions had chilling effects on privacy development, but also accelerated research into compliance-compatible privacy solutions.

Privacy Pools - The Next Generation:
Developed by Ethereum researchers including Vitalik Buterin, Privacy Pools improve on mixers by adding compliance features:
- Users prove they're in the 'good' anonymity set (non-sanctioned funds)
- You can prove your funds aren't from specific sources without revealing their actual source
- Maintains privacy while allowing regulatory compliance
- Balances individual rights with legitimate enforcement needs

Limitations of mixers:

  • Fixed denominations: Having to use 0.1, 1, 10 ETH amounts is inconvenient
  • Timing analysis: Withdrawing soon after depositing can reduce privacy
  • Regulatory risk: Some jurisdictions view mixer use suspiciously
  • Requires many users: Small anonymity sets provide weak privacy
  • One-time use: Only privatizes the single transfer, not ongoing activity

When to use mixers vs alternatives:

  • Mixers: One-time transfers, breaking transaction history, creating fresh wallets
  • Shielded pools (like Railgun): Ongoing private DeFi use, preserving privacy across many transactions
  • Privacy chains (like Zcash, Monero): Comprehensive privacy by default

stealth_addresses.title: Stealth Addresses
stealth_addresses.content:
Stealth addresses let you receive payments to fresh addresses that only you can access, without anyone linking them to your identity or other addresses.

The problem they solve:
Normally when you give someone your Ethereum address to receive payment, they can:
- See all your past transactions and current balance
- Track all future activity on that address
- Connect your identity to that address forever

How stealth addresses work:

  1. You publish a 'stealth meta-address' (a public key)
  2. Sender generates a one-time stealth address from your meta-address
  3. Sender pays to this stealth address
  4. Only you can detect and access funds sent to stealth addresses derived from your meta-address
  5. Observers can't connect the stealth address to you or your other addresses

Technical process (simplified):

  • You have public key P and private key p
  • Sender generates random number r
  • Sender computes stealth address S = P + hash(r × P)
  • You scan blockchain for new stealth addresses using your private key p
  • You can spend from S using derived private key s = p + hash(r × P)

Real implementation - Umbra Cash:

  • Send ETH and tokens to ENS names or addresses privately
  • Recipient gets funds to a fresh address only they control
  • Sender pays ~$5-20 in gas (one-time cost)
  • Works on Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism
  • Over $10 million in private transfers processed

Monero's native implementation:
Monero builds stealth addresses into the protocol:
- Every transaction automatically uses stealth addresses
- No extra cost or complexity for users
- Combined with ring signatures for sender privacy
- Amounts hidden through RingCT (Ring Confidential Transactions)

Result: Complete payment privacy by default. Observers can't see sender, recipient, or amount.

Advantages of stealth addresses:

  • Fresh addresses: Every payment uses a new address
  • No address reuse: Can't link multiple payments to same recipient
  • Works with existing chains: Can be implemented as a layer on top of Ethereum
  • No mixing needed: Privacy without relying on anonymity sets
  • Selective disclosure: You can prove you received a payment if needed

Challenges and limitations:

  • Recipient scanning: You must scan the blockchain to detect payments (though this is improving)
  • Gas costs: Generating stealth addresses costs more gas than regular transfers
  • Doesn't hide amounts: Basic stealth addresses hide sender/recipient but not values
  • Needs wide adoption: More effective when commonly used (privacy through normality)

Future developments:

  • EIP-5564: Proposed Ethereum standard for stealth addresses
  • Wallet integration: Making stealth addresses as easy as normal payments
  • Layer 2 optimization: Reducing costs through rollups
  • Combining with ZKPs: Hiding amounts too, not just addresses

Stealth addresses represent privacy that's user-friendly and practical—a major step toward mainstream adoption of blockchain privacy tools.

encryption.title: Encrypted Smart Contracts and Confidential Computing
encryption.content:
While ZKPs and stealth addresses focus on transaction privacy, encrypted smart contracts enable private computation—running programs on encrypted data without revealing the data itself.

The challenge:
Normal smart contracts execute in public. Every variable, function call, and state change is visible on-chain. This makes privacy-preserving DeFi extremely difficult:
- AMMs: Pool balances and swap amounts are public
- Lending: Collateral amounts and positions visible
- Trading: Limit orders and strategies exposed
- Gaming: All player stats and actions known to everyone

Solution 1: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs)

TEEs are secure hardware enclaves that execute code privately, even from the computer's owner.

Secret Network:

  • Smart contracts run inside Intel SGX secure enclaves
  • Contract state is encrypted on-chain
  • Computations happen privately inside TEE
  • Only encrypted results are stored publicly
  • Use cases: Private DeFi (SecretSwap, Sienna), sealed-bid auctions, confidential voting, private NFT metadata

Oasis Network:

  • Separates consensus layer from ParaTime execution layer
  • ParaTimes can use TEEs for confidential computing
  • Focus on privacy-preserving data tokenization and DeFi
  • Partnerships: Meta, BMW, Chainlink for confidential data applications

Advantages of TEEs:

  • Fast execution (near-native speed)
  • Lower gas costs than ZKP-based privacy
  • Flexible—can run any computation privately
  • Easier for developers than ZKP circuits

Concerns with TEEs:

  • Trust in hardware: Relies on Intel/AMD security (not purely cryptographic)
  • Side-channel attacks: Spectre/Meltdown-style vulnerabilities possible
  • Centralization: Limited hardware manufacturers
  • Not quantum-resistant: Unlike some ZKP schemes

Solution 2: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)

FHE allows computations on encrypted data without decrypting it—the holy grail of privacy technology.

How FHE works:

  1. User encrypts data: Encrypt(5) + Encrypt(3) = Encrypt(8)
  2. Smart contract computes on encrypted values
  3. Result remains encrypted until user decrypts it
  4. Blockchain never sees unencrypted data

Current state of FHE:

  • Still early: FHE is extremely computationally expensive (1000x-1000000x slower than normal computation)
  • Research active: Zama, Sunscreen, Fhenix working on blockchain FHE
  • Hybrid approaches: Combining FHE with ZKPs and TEEs for practical performance

Solution 3: Multi-Party Computation (MPC)

MPC splits private data across multiple parties who jointly compute results without any party seeing the full data.

Applications in blockchain:

  • Threshold signatures: Requiring M-of-N parties to sign (used in TSS wallets)
  • Private auctions: Determining winner without revealing losing bids
  • Confidential voting: Counting votes without revealing individual choices
  • Privacy-preserving analytics: Computing aggregate stats without revealing individual data

Real example - Fairyproof:
Decentralized KYC where your identity data is split across multiple nodes. You can prove you're KYC'd without revealing data to any single party or the blockchain.

The future—combining approaches:

Cutting-edge privacy systems combine multiple technologies:

  • Aztec: ZKPs for transaction privacy + encrypted UTXO model
  • Railgun: zk-SNARKs + private balances + public DeFi interaction
  • Penumbra: ZKPs + threshold encryption + IBC privacy

As these technologies mature and become cheaper, we'll see privacy become standard rather than exceptional in blockchain applications.

privacy_tools.title: Privacy Tools and Protocols
privacy_tools.content: From early mixers to modern ZK-powered platforms, privacy tools have evolved dramatically. Understanding their history, capabilities, and trade-offs helps you choose the right solution.

tornado_cash_history.title: Tornado Cash and the Fight for Privacy
tornado_cash_history.content:
Tornado Cash was the most popular Ethereum mixer, processing over $7 billion in volume from 2019-2022. Its story illustrates both the potential and challenges of blockchain privacy.

How it worked:

  • Deposit ETH or tokens into a pool (fixed amounts: 0.1, 1, 10, 100 ETH)
  • Receive a secret cryptographic note proving your deposit
  • Wait for more deposits to increase anonymity set
  • Withdraw to a fresh address using the note
  • zk-SNARK proves you made a valid deposit without revealing which one

Legitimate use cases:

  • Protecting donation privacy (to avoid doxing supporters)
  • Salary privacy (employees not revealing income to everyone)
  • Breaking transaction history when moving from exchange to cold storage
  • Protecting businesses from competitor surveillance
  • Whistleblower and journalist protection

The sanctions and aftermath:
On August 8, 2022, the U.S. Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned Tornado Cash, alleging it laundered over $455 million for North Korean hackers and other criminals.

Immediate effects:

  • Tornado Cash website taken down
  • GitHub repositories removed (later restored)
  • Developer Alexey Pertsev arrested in Netherlands
  • RPC providers blocked access to Tornado contracts
  • DeFi protocols blacklisted addresses that interacted with Tornado

Controversy and legal challenges:

The sanctions raised unprecedented questions:

  • Can code be sanctioned? Tornado is an immutable smart contract, not a company or person
  • Is privacy illegal? Most users (~90%) were legitimate privacy seekers, not criminals
  • Due process concerns: People who received unsolicited Tornado dust got sanctioned addresses
  • Chilling effects: Other privacy developers feared prosecution

Community response:

  • Coin Center and other advocates filed lawsuits challenging sanctions
  • Privacy research accelerated toward compliance-compatible solutions
  • Forks and alternatives emerged (though with regulatory uncertainty)

Lessons learned:

  1. Privacy needs compliance tools: Pure anonymity is legally risky; selective disclosure is better
  2. Immutable contracts have limits: Even unstoppable code faces social/legal pressure
  3. Privacy is a spectrum: From full transparency to complete anonymity, most users need something in between
  4. Education matters: Better communication about privacy rights vs. criminal use

Current status (as of 2025):

  • Legal challenges ongoing in U.S. courts
  • Developer trials in Netherlands progressing
  • Smart contracts still functional but rarely used (due to legal risk)
  • Privacy development shifted to compliance-first designs

case_sanctions.title: OFAC Sanctions Tornado Cash
case_sanctions.description: On August 8, 2022, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned Tornado Cash, marking the first time the government sanctioned a smart contract rather than a person or entity. The action alleged Tornado Cash laundered over $7 billion, including $455 million stolen by North Korean hackers. This unprecedented move sparked intense debate about privacy rights, code as speech, and the limits of government authority over decentralized protocols. Legal challenges are ongoing, with major implications for blockchain privacy development.

railgun.title: Railgun - Private DeFi Protocol
railgun.content:
Railgun is a privacy system built on Ethereum that lets you interact with DeFi while keeping your balances and actions private. Unlike mixers, Railgun creates a persistent shielded pool where you can hold funds and use them with any DeFi protocol.

Key innovation:
Most privacy tools force a choice: either use DeFi publicly or stay in a privacy pool isolated from DeFi. Railgun bridges this gap—you can swap on Uniswap, lend on Aave, or provide liquidity to Curve while maintaining privacy.

How Railgun works:

  1. Shield: Deposit ETH or tokens into Railgun's private system
  2. Private balance: Your holdings are encrypted on-chain, only you can decrypt them
  3. Private actions: Swap, transfer, or interact with contracts privately
  4. Unshield: Withdraw to a public address when needed

All operations use zk-SNARKs to prove validity without revealing amounts, addresses, or actions.

Technical architecture:

  • Private balances: UTXO model like Bitcoin but encrypted
  • Merkle tree: All private transactions added to a tree structure
  • Nullifiers: Prevent double-spending without revealing which UTXO was spent
  • Relayers: Submit transactions on your behalf to hide originating address

Supported features:

  • Private transfers of ETH and ERC-20 tokens
  • Private swaps through DEXs (Uniswap, Sushiswap, etc.)
  • Private DeFi interactions (lending, borrowing, LPing)
  • Cross-chain: Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum, BSC

Privacy guarantees:

  • Hidden amounts: Nobody can see your balance or transaction sizes
  • Hidden recipients: Transfers don't reveal who received funds
  • Hidden actions: DeFi interactions don't show what you did
  • Private history: Your transaction graph is hidden

Compliance features:

Learning from Tornado Cash, Railgun built in privacy-preserving compliance:

  • Private Proof of Innocence (PPOI): Prove your funds didn't come from sanctioned sources without revealing their actual source
  • Decentralized screening: Community-run compliance without central authority
  • Selective disclosure: Optional viewing keys to prove balances/transactions to auditors

Use cases:

  • Salary privacy: Receive and spend without employer seeing your total wealth
  • Business operations: Protect trade secrets and supplier relationships
  • Trading strategies: Prevent copycats and MEV exploitation
  • Donation privacy: Support causes without public association

Trade-offs:

  • Gas costs: ZK proofs cost more gas (~$10-50 per transaction on Ethereum mainnet)
  • Proof generation time: 30-60 seconds to generate proofs locally
  • Complexity: More steps than normal DeFi transactions
  • Liquidity: Smaller private pools than public DeFi

Statistics (as of 2025):

  • Over $1 billion in total value shielded
  • Supports 100+ tokens across multiple chains
  • Thousands of active private wallets
  • Zero exploits or hacks since launch

Railgun represents the next generation of privacy tools: practical, compliance-compatible, and integrated with the broader DeFi ecosystem.

aztec.title: Aztec - Encrypted Rollup
aztec.content:
Aztec is building an encrypted zkRollup—an entire Layer 2 blockchain where all state and execution are encrypted by default. It's the most ambitious privacy project in the Ethereum ecosystem.

The vision:
Instead of building privacy tools on top of transparent blockchains, Aztec creates a blockchain where privacy is built-in at the protocol level. Every transaction, smart contract state, and account balance is encrypted.

Architecture evolution:

Aztec Connect (2022-2023):

  • Privacy rollup connecting to public Ethereum DeFi
  • Let users privately interact with Curve, Aave, Lido, etc.
  • Processed over $400 million in private volume
  • Sunset in mid-2023 to focus on full encrypted rollup

Aztec 3.0 (current development):

  • Fully encrypted zkRollup with private smart contracts
  • New programming language: Noir (for writing ZK circuits)
  • Private state, private functions, private execution
  • Selective disclosure and composability

Key innovations:

1. Private smart contracts:
Contracts can have both public and private state:
- Public state: Visible to everyone (like normal Ethereum)
- Private state: Encrypted, only accessible with permission
- Developers choose what's public vs private per function

2. Noir language:
New language for writing zero-knowledge circuits:
- Easier than writing raw ZK circuits
- Compiles to zk-SNARK proofs
- Growing ecosystem of libraries and tools
- Can be used beyond Aztec (portable ZK circuits)

3. Private-public composability:
Aztec contracts can interact with public Ethereum seamlessly:
- Private Aztec transaction triggers public Ethereum action
- Or vice versa
- Enables private DeFi using public liquidity

Example use case - Private DEX:

  1. User submits private swap intent to Aztec
  2. Aztec contract verifies user has sufficient balance (privately)
  3. Contract executes swap against public Ethereum liquidity pool
  4. User receives tokens privately in Aztec

Result: Trading with public liquidity but private amounts and account balances.

Technical details:

  • PLONK proofs: Advanced zk-SNARK system with universal trusted setup
  • Encrypted state model: Contract state stored as encrypted notes
  • Private kernels: Proving system for private execution
  • Recursive proofs: Proving validity of other proofs for scalability

Development status (2025):

  • Mainnet in public testnet phase
  • Developer documentation and tooling maturing
  • Several projects building on Aztec
  • Aiming for production mainnet in 2025

Potential applications:

  • Private DeFi: All DeFi actions with balance privacy
  • Confidential business logic: Smart contracts with trade secrets
  • Private gaming: On-chain games where player state is hidden
  • Sealed-bid auctions: True sealed bids enforced cryptographically
  • Private DAOs: Governance voting with ballot secrecy

Challenges ahead:

  • Performance: ZK proof generation still slow for complex contracts
  • Developer adoption: Learning Noir and ZK concepts is challenging
  • Network effects: Needs critical mass of users and developers
  • Regulatory uncertainty: Will encrypted rollups face legal pressure?

If successful, Aztec could prove that blockchains can be both transparent (for verification) and private (for users)—the best of both worlds.

privacy_chains.title: Privacy-First Blockchains
privacy_chains.content:
While Ethereum projects add privacy on top of transparent blockchains, some chains built privacy into their DNA from day one. These privacy chains prove that financial confidentiality and blockchain verification can coexist.

Zcash - The ZK Pioneer:

History:
Launched in 2016 by cryptographers including Zcash inventor (and Turing Award winner) Silvio Micali. First blockchain to use zk-SNARKs in production.

How it works:

  • Two types of addresses: Transparent (like Bitcoin) and Shielded (private)
  • Shielded transactions: Hide sender, recipient, and amount using zk-SNARKs
  • Selective disclosure: Viewing keys and payment disclosures let you prove transactions when needed
  • Memo field: Encrypted messages attached to shielded transactions

Privacy guarantees:
A fully shielded Zcash transaction reveals zero information publicly. Observers see that a valid transaction occurred, but nothing about who sent to whom or how much.

Statistics:

  • Over $30 billion in shielded volume since launch
  • ~30% of ZEC in shielded pool (as of 2025)
  • No known privacy breaks or exploits

Compliance features:

  • Viewing keys: Let auditors see your transactions without spending power
  • Payment disclosure: Prove specific transaction details selectively
  • Addresses visible when needed: Can use transparent addresses for public accountability

Monero - Default Privacy:

Philosophy:
Unlike Zcash (opt-in privacy), Monero makes all transactions private by default. You can't accidentally reveal your balance or history.

Technologies:

  • Ring signatures: Your transaction is signed by a group, observers can't tell who the real signer is
  • Stealth addresses: Every transaction uses a one-time address, hiding recipients
  • RingCT: Ring Confidential Transactions hide amounts
  • Dandelion++: Network-layer privacy to hide transaction origin

Result:
Complete privacy for all users, all the time. No option for transparent transactions.

Trade-offs:

  • Exchange delistings: Many exchanges dropped Monero due to regulatory pressure
  • Compliance impossible: Can't selectively disclose for audits (by design)
  • Blockchain size: Privacy features make chain larger (~150GB+)
  • Verification time: Proving transaction validity takes longer than Bitcoin

Use cases:
Monero is favored by privacy advocates, journalists, activists, and anyone needing financial confidentiality without compromise. However, regulatory hostility limits mainstream adoption.

Iron Fish - Encrypted PoW:

Newer privacy chain (launched 2023) combining proven privacy tech with modern design:

  • zk-SNARKs for transaction privacy (like Zcash)
  • Proof of Work consensus (like Bitcoin)
  • Privacy by default (like Monero)
  • Built for compliance (viewing keys standard)

Comparison - Privacy Chains vs Privacy Tools:

Privacy chains (Zcash, Monero, Iron Fish):

  • Pros: Privacy built-in, usually cheaper transactions, simpler UX
  • Cons: Less DeFi ecosystem, harder to exchange, regulatory pressure, need to hold native token

Privacy tools on Ethereum (Railgun, Aztec):

  • Pros: Access to full DeFi ecosystem, use ETH and existing tokens, better liquidity
  • Cons: Higher costs, more complex, privacy features added on top rather than native

The future of privacy chains:

As regulatory frameworks mature, we may see privacy chains with built-in compliance features become acceptable. The key is designing systems that:
1. Protect ordinary users' financial privacy
2. Prevent large-scale money laundering
3. Allow selective disclosure for legitimate needs
4. Maintain decentralization and censorship resistance

Privacy chains prove the technology works. The remaining challenges are primarily social, legal, and economic rather than technical.

private_transactions.title: How to Send Private Transactions
private_transactions.content: Theory is important, but practical knowledge is what protects your privacy. Here's how to actually send private transactions and use privacy-preserving DeFi.

how_to_send.title: Step-by-Step: Private Transfers
how_to_send.content:
Let's walk through sending a private payment using different privacy tools. We'll compare ease of use, cost, and privacy guarantees.

Method 1: Railgun Private Transfer

Setup (one-time):

  1. Install Railway wallet (Railgun's official wallet) or use WalletConnect from supported wallets
  2. Generate your Railgun private address (0zk...)
  3. Fund your wallet with ETH for gas fees

Shielding assets:

  1. Click 'Shield' in Railway wallet
  2. Select token and amount to make private
  3. Confirm transaction (costs gas + generates ZK proof)
  4. Wait ~1 minute for proof generation
  5. After confirmation, funds are in private balance

Private transfer:

  1. Click 'Send Private'
  2. Enter recipient's Railgun address (0zk...) or ENS name
  3. Specify amount
  4. Generate proof (~30-60 seconds)
  5. Submit transaction

Result:
- On-chain: Only 'a transaction occurred to Railgun contract' is visible
- Sender address: Hidden
- Recipient address: Hidden
- Amount: Hidden
- Costs: ~$20-50 on Ethereum mainnet, ~$1-5 on Polygon/Arbitrum

Method 2: Umbra Stealth Payments

Setup:

  1. Connect wallet to Umbra.cash
  2. Register your stealth meta-address (one-time, ~$5 gas)

Sending:

  1. Enter recipient's ENS name or stealth meta-address
  2. Specify amount and token
  3. Click 'Send'
  4. Confirm transaction

Receiving:

  1. Visit Umbra.cash and scan for payments
  2. Any payments to your stealth addresses will appear
  3. Withdraw to any address you choose

Result:
- Funds sent to one-time address only recipient can access
- Sender/recipient relationship hidden
- Amount visible on-chain (not hidden by default)
- Costs: ~$10-30 on Ethereum mainnet

Method 3: Cross-Chain Privacy Bridge

For maximum privacy when moving between chains:

  1. Shield on source chain (e.g., Ethereum Railgun)
  2. Transfer privately to any private address
  3. Bridge to destination chain while staying shielded
  4. Unshield to fresh address on destination chain

Result:
On-chain observers can't connect your source address to destination address.

Privacy best practices for transfers:

  • Timing: Don't shield and immediately unshield (reduces anonymity set)
  • Amounts: Avoid unique amounts that might identify you (don't send 1.23456789 ETH)
  • Addresses: Unshield to fresh addresses with no prior transaction history
  • Gas: Fund new addresses with gas from different source than shielded funds
  • Chain analysis: Assume sophisticated adversaries can correlate timing/amounts across chains

Common mistakes to avoid:

  • ❌ Shielding directly from KYC exchange to private wallet
  • ✅ Shield from KYC exchange → wait → unshield to intermediate address → wait → shield again → private transfers
  • ❌ Using same ENS name for public and private addresses
  • ✅ Create separate identity for private transactions
  • ❌ Tweeting about your private transactions ('just sent X privately!')
  • ✅ Never publicly associate your identity with private addresses

private_defi.title: Private DeFi Operations
private_defi.content:
Beyond simple transfers, you can interact with DeFi protocols while maintaining privacy. This is more complex but enables private trading, lending, and liquidity provision.

Private Swapping with Railgun:

  1. Ensure you have shielded tokens in Railgun
  2. Select 'Private Swap' in Railway wallet
  3. Choose input and output tokens
  4. Swap executes through public DEX but with private amounts
  5. Receive swapped tokens in private balance

How it works under the hood:

  1. You have private USDC balance in Railgun
  2. Generate ZK proof: 'I have X USDC and want to swap for ETH'
  3. Railgun contract calls Uniswap publicly
  4. Swap executes at current market rate
  5. ETH is deposited back to private balance
  6. On-chain: Shows 'Railgun contract swapped on Uniswap' but not amounts or user

Private Lending:

Using Secret Network's private lending protocols:

  1. Bridge assets to Secret Network
  2. Wrap to private SNIP-20 token standard
  3. Deposit to lending protocol (e.g., Sienna Lend)
  4. Borrow against collateral privately

Privacy guarantees:

  • Your collateral amount: Hidden
  • Borrowed amount: Hidden
  • Liquidation risk: Hidden from other users (but protocol knows internally)
  • Position size: Hidden

Use case:
Whales can borrow stables against ETH collateral without revealing position size. Prevents copycat trading and liquidation hunting.

Private Liquidity Provision:

Providing liquidity without revealing position size:

  1. Use Railgun to privately swap to 50/50 split of pool tokens
  2. Add liquidity through Railgun to public pool (e.g., Uniswap)
  3. LP tokens minted to private Railgun balance
  4. Collect fees privately over time
  5. Remove liquidity privately

Benefits:

  • Competitors can't see your LP positions
  • No one knows your fee earnings
  • Position size remains confidential

Private Trading Strategies:

Strategy 1: Private Accumulation
Accumulating a position without moving the market:

  1. Split capital across multiple fresh addresses
  2. Use each address once to swap through Railgun
  3. Accumulate target token in private balance
  4. Nobody knows you're accumulating (unlike public address doing 50 buys)

Strategy 2: Private Limit Orders
Using CoW Swap for private order flow:

  1. Place limit order on CoW Swap
  2. Order isn't published to public mempool
  3. Solvers match your order off-chain when price is hit
  4. Execute on-chain only when filled
  5. Your trading intent never visible to frontrunners

Private DeFi Costs:

Privacy isn't free. Typical costs:

  • Shield/Unshield: $10-50 per operation (Ethereum mainnet)
  • Private transfers: $15-40
  • Private swaps: $30-80
  • L2 costs: 10-20x cheaper on Polygon, Arbitrum

When private DeFi is worth it:

  • Position size: $10,000+ (costs become negligible percentage)
  • Frequency: Regular DeFi users (one-time shield cost amortizes)
  • Risk: High-value traders who face MEV/copycats
  • Privacy needs: Anyone who wants financial confidentiality

When it might not be worth it:

  • Small trades: $100 swap with $50 privacy cost doesn't make sense
  • One-time users: Privacy costs exceed MEV savings for casual users
  • Public protocols: Some DeFi actions need to be public (e.g., governance voting)

best_practices.title: Privacy Best Practices
best_practices.content:
Technology is only half the battle. Maintaining privacy requires operational security and understanding how privacy can be compromised.

Address Hygiene:

  • Fresh addresses: Use new address for each unshielding operation
  • No reuse: Never deposit back to an address you've used publicly
  • Separate identities: Different addresses for public DeFi vs private operations
  • Gas management: Fund fresh addresses from non-linked sources

Timing and Amount Correlation:

Chain analysis can correlate transactions by timing and amounts:

  • ❌ Shield 12.345 ETH, wait 2 minutes, unshield 12.345 ETH
  • ✅ Shield 12.345 ETH, wait days, unshield 8.2 ETH and 4.1 ETH separately
  • ❌ Shield at 10:00 AM, unshield at 10:05 AM (every day same time)
  • ✅ Randomize timing, wait variable durations

Cross-Chain Correlation:

Bridge transactions can leak privacy:

  • ❌ Shield ETH → bridge to Polygon → immediately unshield
  • ✅ Shield ETH → wait → bridge → wait → split into multiple amounts → wait → unshield

Metadata Leakage:

Privacy tools hide on-chain data but other data can leak:

  • IP addresses: Use VPN or Tor when connecting to wallets
  • RPC providers: They see your wallet requests (use privacy-focused RPCs)
  • Browser fingerprinting: Websites can track you beyond wallet addresses
  • Social connections: Don't tweet about private transactions or addresses

Anonymity Set Size:

Your privacy depends on how many others use the same pool:

  • Large pools: Better privacy (1-in-10,000 ambiguity)
  • Small pools: Weaker privacy (1-in-10 ambiguity)
  • Unique amounts: If you're the only one who shielded 123.456 ETH, timing analysis can identify you

Selective Disclosure:

Sometimes you need to prove transaction details:

  • Viewing keys: Share read-only access to specific transactions (Zcash, Railgun)
  • Payment proofs: Prove you sent specific amount to specific recipient
  • Balance proofs: Prove you hold certain amount without revealing exact balance
  • Compliance proofs: Prove funds aren't from sanctioned sources (Railgun PPOI)

Threat Modeling:

Who are you protecting privacy from?

  • Casual observers: Basic privacy tools sufficient
  • Sophisticated chain analysis: Need careful timing, amount randomization
  • Nation-state adversaries: Require operational security beyond just privacy tools
  • Legal compliance: Use tools with built-in compliance features

Privacy Toolkit:

  • VPN/Tor: Hide IP when transacting
  • Private RPC: Use your own node or privacy-focused providers
  • Fresh devices: Don't use same browser/device for private and public identities
  • Encrypted communications: Discuss addresses/transactions over Signal, not Twitter
  • Hardware wallets: Prevent key leakage from compromised computers

Red Flags - When Privacy is Compromised:

  • Exchange asks where your private transaction funds came from
  • Someone correctly identifies your private transaction
  • Tax authority questions undisclosed private holdings
  • Social engineering attempts based on your supposed private activities

Recovery and Incident Response:

If privacy is compromised:

  1. Stop using compromised addresses immediately
  2. Don't try to 'fix' by mixing more (makes it worse)
  3. Create completely fresh identity with new addresses
  4. Learn from the mistake and improve operational security

Privacy is a practice, not a product. The best privacy tools fail if you make operational security mistakes. Stay vigilant, keep learning, and remember: privacy is a right, not a privilege.

compliance_balance.title: Balancing Privacy and Compliance
compliance_balance.content: The Tornado Cash sanctions highlighted a core tension: privacy is a right, but authorities need tools to prevent money laundering and terrorism financing. The future of blockchain privacy depends on finding solutions that protect individuals while addressing legitimate regulatory concerns.

regulatory_landscape.title: Understanding the Regulatory Landscape
regulatory_landscape.content:
Privacy tools operate in a complex legal environment that varies dramatically by jurisdiction and changes rapidly.

United States:

  • OFAC sanctions: Can target addresses, protocols, or even code
  • FinCEN guidance: Mixers and tumblers treated as money transmitters (requiring licensing)
  • Bank Secrecy Act: Financial institutions must report suspicious activity
  • Travel Rule: Crypto transfers over $3,000 must include sender/recipient info

European Union:

  • AMLD5/6: Anti-money laundering directives covering crypto
  • MiCA: Markets in Crypto Assets regulation (2024+)
  • GDPR: Data privacy rights (sometimes conflicts with blockchain transparency)
  • Transfer of Funds Regulation: Similar to U.S. Travel Rule

Other jurisdictions:

  • Singapore: Supportive of privacy tech with compliance features
  • Switzerland: Privacy-friendly but requires AML compliance
  • China: Banned privacy coins and anonymous transactions
  • UAE: Developing crypto regulations, privacy status unclear

Key regulatory concerns:

  1. Money laundering: Using privacy tools to hide proceeds of crime
  2. Terrorism financing: Anonymous transactions funding terrorist organizations
  3. Tax evasion: Hiding income and capital gains from tax authorities
  4. Sanctions evasion: Circumventing OFAC and other sanctions programs

Legitimate counterarguments:

  • Privacy tools used 90%+ by legitimate users, not criminals
  • Cash provides similar privacy but isn't banned
  • Financial privacy is recognized human right (UN Declaration)
  • Surveillance creates more problems than it solves (oppression, theft, exploitation)

The data on privacy tool usage:

Chainalysis 2023 report on Tornado Cash (before sanctions):

  • ~17% of volume from known illicit sources
  • ~83% from presumably legitimate privacy seekers
  • Most illicit volume: Hacks and thefts (not drugs/terrorism)

Compare to traditional finance:

  • UN estimates 2-5% of global GDP is laundered ($800B-$2T annually)
  • Crypto represents tiny fraction of money laundering globally

Legal risk levels for users:

Low risk:

  • Using privacy chains (Zcash, Monero) in jurisdictions where they're legal
  • Privacy tools with compliance features (Railgun PPOI, Privacy Pools)
  • Stealth addresses for legitimate privacy
  • VPNs and privacy-preserving browsers

Medium risk:

  • Large amounts through mixers (may trigger AML alerts)
  • Privacy tools in jurisdictions with unclear regulations
  • Frequent privacy tool usage (pattern detection)

High risk:

  • Using sanctioned protocols (Tornado Cash in U.S.)
  • Privacy tools in hostile jurisdictions (China, etc.)
  • Mixing after receiving funds from known criminal source
  • Cannot explain source of funds to regulators

compliant_privacy.title: Privacy with Compliance
compliant_privacy.content:
The next generation of privacy tools is being designed with compliance in mind from the start. These solutions aim to protect legitimate privacy while preventing abuse.

Privacy Pools - Vitalik's Solution:

Proposed by Vitalik Buterin and Jacob Illum in 2023, Privacy Pools add compliance to mixing technology.

How they work:

  1. Users deposit funds into privacy pool (like Tornado Cash)
  2. When withdrawing, user proves they're in the 'good' subset
  3. 'Good' subset: All users except sanctioned addresses/known criminals
  4. Proof reveals nothing about actual source, just that it's not from excluded set

Technical mechanism:

  • Each user has membership in anonymity set
  • Users create association sets (who they're willing to be associated with)
  • ZK proof shows: 'I'm in the approved set' without revealing which member
  • Can satisfy compliance without sacrificing privacy

Benefits:

  • Legitimate users get privacy
  • Criminals/sanctioned addresses excluded (provably)
  • Regulators can verify exclusion of bad actors
  • Users not tainted by others' bad behavior

Railgun's Private Proof of Innocence (PPOI):

Live implementation of compliance-compatible privacy.

How PPOI works:

  1. Railgun users shield assets into private system
  2. Community-run screening checks sources against sanctions lists
  3. Users generate ZK proof of passing screening
  4. Proof required to unshield to exchanges/regulated entities
  5. Proof reveals nothing except 'funds passed compliance check'

Decentralized compliance:

  • No central authority deciding who's compliant
  • Open-source screening criteria
  • Users can verify screening is fair
  • Privacy and compliance both maintained

Real-world acceptance:
Several exchanges now accept PPOI proofs, showing the model can work in practice.

Selective Disclosure Mechanisms:

Multiple privacy systems now support revealing information when needed:

Zcash viewing keys:

  • Share read-only access to specific transactions
  • Can give to auditors, tax authorities, regulators
  • Doesn't compromise spending keys or future privacy

Railgun viewing keys:

  • Prove specific transactions or balances
  • Can show 'funds came from clean source' without revealing exact source
  • Time-limited disclosure possible

Payment disclosure:

  • Prove you sent specific amount to specific recipient
  • Useful for business receipts, proof of donation, etc.
  • Selective—doesn't reveal entire transaction history

Institutional Compliance Solutions:

For businesses needing privacy with full compliance:

  • Fireblocks: Institutional custody with transaction screening
  • Chainalysis integration: Privacy tools integrating chain analysis for risk scoring
  • VASP systems: Travel Rule compliance for privacy-preserving transfers

Future compliance innovations:

  • ZK-KYC: Prove you're KYC'd without revealing identity
  • Threshold compliance: Multi-party computation for privacy + AML
  • Programmable compliance: Smart contracts enforcing rules while maintaining privacy
  • Decentralized identity: Portable compliance credentials

selective_disclosure.title: Selective Disclosure and Transparency
selective_disclosure.content:
The best privacy systems give users control over what they reveal and to whom. This puts power in individuals' hands rather than making blanket privacy or transparency decisions.

The Spectrum of Disclosure:

Full Privacy (Monero model):

  • Everything hidden, no exceptions
  • Protects against all surveillance
  • Cannot comply with audits or regulations
  • Use case: Maximum privacy advocates, jurisdictions with oppressive surveillance

Selective Disclosure (Zcash model):

  • Default privacy, optional disclosure
  • Viewing keys for specific audits
  • Payment proofs when needed
  • Use case: Businesses, compliant privacy users, flexible needs

Programmable Privacy (Future vision):

  • Fine-grained disclosure rules
  • Automatic compliance proofs
  • Time-limited disclosure
  • Use case: Institutional DeFi, regulated privacy

Practical selective disclosure scenarios:

Scenario 1: Tax Compliance

  1. You conduct private transactions all year
  2. Tax season arrives
  3. Generate viewing key for tax authority
  4. Tax authority sees your relevant transactions
  5. File taxes accurately while maintaining privacy from public

Scenario 2: Business Audit

  1. Company uses private DeFi for operations
  2. Annual audit required
  3. Generate time-limited viewing key for auditor
  4. Auditor verifies financials without seeing trade secrets
  5. After audit, viewing access expires automatically

Scenario 3: Proof of Solvency

  1. DeFi protocol holds user funds privately
  2. Users want proof protocol is solvent
  3. Protocol generates ZK proof: 'We hold ≥ X amount'
  4. Proves solvency without revealing exact holdings or addresses
  5. Users reassured, privacy maintained

    6. Technical implementations:

    Viewing keys (Zcash):

    - Full viewing key: See all transactions
    - Incoming viewing key: See received payments only
    - Outgoing viewing key: See sent payments only
    - Payment disclosure key: Prove specific transaction

    Zero-knowledge disclosures:

    • Prove balance > $X without revealing exact balance
    • Prove transaction occurred between dates without revealing details
    • Prove membership in compliant set without revealing which member
    • Prove funds from legitimate source without revealing source

    Time-based disclosure:

    • Viewing access that expires after audit period
    • Progressive disclosure (more info revealed over time)
    • Emergency disclosure (decrypt if certain conditions met)

    Multi-party disclosure:

    • Require M-of-N parties to combine for disclosure
    • Prevents single party from accessing data
    • Useful for escrow, dispute resolution, compliance

    Future: Programmable Privacy

    Smart contracts that enforce privacy rules:

    if (user.isKYC && transaction.isLegitimate) {
      allow(transaction, privacy=HIGH);
    } else if (user.requestsDisclosure) {
      allow(transaction, privacy=SELECTIVE);
    } else {
      deny(transaction);
    }

    This vision combines:

    • Privacy by default for compliant users
    • Automatic exclusion of sanctioned addresses
    • Flexible disclosure for legitimate needs
    • User control over their data

    The goal: Privacy that adapts to context. Full privacy against surveillance, selective disclosure for compliance, emergency disclosure for legal process. Users in control, not systems or authorities.

risks.title: Privacy Risks and Considerations
risks.content: Privacy tools provide powerful protection, but they're not magic. Understanding their limitations and risks is crucial for using them safely and effectively.

technical_risks.title: Technical Risks
technical_risks.content:
Privacy technologies are cutting-edge cryptography. While generally secure, they have unique technical risks.

Smart Contract Risks:

  • Code exploits: Privacy contracts are complex, bugs can lead to fund loss
  • Trusted setup issues: zk-SNARKs require trusted setup ceremonies (if compromised, privacy breaks)
  • Upgradeability concerns: Some contracts upgradeable, creating centralization risk

Historical example - Zcash trusted setup:
Zcash's initial zk-SNARK parameters required a trusted setup ceremony in 2016. If the 'toxic waste' from this ceremony wasn't destroyed properly, someone could counterfeit shielded ZEC undetectably.

Zcash performed an elaborate ceremony with six participants, each independently destroying their portion. The chance all six colluded or were compromised is extremely low, but the risk existed.

Cryptographic Risks:

  • Quantum computers: Could break zk-SNARKs in future (though zk-STARKs are quantum-resistant)
  • Cryptographic breaks: New mathematical discoveries could compromise privacy
  • Implementation bugs: Correct cryptography implemented incorrectly

Network-Level Risks:

  • IP tracking: Privacy tools hide on-chain data but not network metadata
  • RPC surveillance: RPC providers see your requests and can link addresses
  • Timing analysis: Observing when transactions submitted can reduce privacy
  • Sybil attacks: Adversary controlling many nodes to track transactions

Operational Risks:

  • Key management: Losing private keys = losing private funds (no recovery possible usually)
  • Proof generation: Crashes during proof generation can leave funds in limbo
  • Wallet bugs: Privacy wallet software is newer and less tested than standard wallets

Mitigation strategies:

  • Use well-audited protocols (Railgun: 8+ audits, Zcash: 9+ audits)
  • Start with small amounts to test
  • Keep private keys in hardware wallets
  • Use VPNs/Tor for network privacy
  • Run your own node for RPC (eliminates provider tracking)

legal_risks.title: Legal and Regulatory Risks
legal_risks.content:
The legal landscape for privacy tools is uncertain and hostile in many jurisdictions. Users face real legal risks.

Current legal risks:

1. Sanctions violations:

  • Using OFAC-sanctioned protocols (Tornado Cash in U.S.)
  • Interacting with sanctioned addresses
  • Helping others evade sanctions
  • Penalties: Fines, asset seizure, criminal prosecution

2. Money laundering charges:

  • Operating unlicensed money transmission (if running privacy service)
  • Knowingly mixing criminal proceeds
  • Structuring transactions to evade reporting
  • Penalties: Up to 20 years prison (U.S.)

3. Tax evasion:

  • Hiding income/gains using privacy tools
  • Failing to report crypto holdings
  • Not paying taxes on private transactions
  • Penalties: Fines, back taxes, criminal charges

4. Securities violations:

  • Privacy coin offerings treated as unregistered securities
  • Promoting privacy tokens without registration
  • Penalties: SEC enforcement actions

Real cases:

Alexey Pertsev (Tornado Cash developer):

  • Arrested August 2022 in Netherlands
  • Charged with facilitating money laundering
  • Held in custody for months
  • Trial ongoing as of 2025
  • Controversial: Pertsev wrote code, didn't launder money himself

Roman Storm (Tornado Cash developer):

  • U.S. charges: Conspiracy to launder money, sanctions violations
  • Accused of helping users evade sanctions
  • Faces decades in prison if convicted
  • Case raises questions about developer liability for user actions

Helix mixer operator:

  • Ran Bitcoin mixer on darknet
  • Convicted of money laundering
  • Sentenced to 3 years prison (2021)

Jurisdictional risks:

High-risk jurisdictions (hostile to privacy):

  • United States (post-Tornado sanctions)
  • China (privacy coins banned)
  • India (attempting to ban private cryptocurrencies)

Medium-risk (uncertain):

  • European Union (moving toward regulation)
  • United Kingdom (following EU approach)
  • South Korea (monitoring privacy tools)

Lower-risk (more permissive):

  • Switzerland (privacy-friendly)
  • Singapore (balanced approach)
  • Portugal (generally crypto-friendly)

How to manage legal risk:

  1. Know your jurisdiction: Research local laws on privacy tools
  2. Use compliance features: PPOI, viewing keys, payment proofs
  3. Document legitimate use: Keep records of why you need privacy
  4. Consult tax attorney: Ensure you're reporting properly
  5. Start small: Test with small amounts before committing large sums
  6. Stay informed: Laws change rapidly, keep up with developments

When to avoid privacy tools:

  • You're in jurisdiction that banned them
  • You can't explain source of funds to authorities
  • Funds actually are from criminal activity (don't do crimes)
  • You're risk-averse and legal uncertainty concerns you

When privacy tools are justified:

  • Legitimate privacy needs (salary, business, donations)
  • Operating in compliant way (using PPOI, reporting taxes)
  • Jurisdiction hasn't banned privacy tools
  • You're willing to accept legal uncertainty for privacy benefits

anonymity_set.title: Anonymity Set Limitations
anonymity_set.content:
Your privacy is only as strong as the anonymity set you're part of. Understanding these limitations prevents false sense of security.

What is an anonymity set?

The group of users who could plausibly be you. If 1,000 people used a privacy pool and you're one of them, you have 1-in-1,000 anonymity (pretty good). If only 10 people used it, you have 1-in-10 anonymity (weak).

Factors reducing anonymity sets:

1. Unique amounts:

  • If you shield 12.34567890 ETH and someone unshields 12.34567890 ETH, probably the same person
  • Even with delays, unique amounts are fingerprintable
  • Solution: Use common amounts, split into multiple transactions

2. Timing correlation:

  • Shielding and unshielding within short timeframe reduces anonymity
  • Predictable timing patterns (e.g., every Monday at 10am) fingerprintable
  • Solution: Wait variable random durations, avoid patterns

3. Cross-chain correlation:

  • Bridging between chains can leak timing/amount correlations
  • Using same amounts across chains reduces anonymity
  • Solution: Split amounts, wait between chain hops, randomize

4. Small anonymity sets:

  • New privacy pools with few users provide weak privacy
  • Niche tokens with small user base easier to trace
  • Solution: Use established pools with thousands of users

Real-world anonymity set analysis:

Tornado Cash 100 ETH pool (before sanctions):

  • ~5,000 total deposits historically
  • ~100-200 active users per month
  • If you withdraw same month you deposit: 1-in-100 anonymity
  • If you wait 6 months: 1-in-1,000+ anonymity

Railgun shielded pool:

  • Thousands of shielded addresses
  • Millions in TVL across multiple tokens
  • Variable amounts (not fixed denominations)
  • Harder to analyze but also harder to use correctly

Advanced deanonymization techniques:

Timing analysis:

  • Observing mempool for shield/unshield timing
  • Correlating user activity patterns across time
  • Success rate: Can narrow to 10-100 candidates often

Amount analysis:

  • Tracking unique amount patterns
  • Gas amount correlations (same gas prices = possibly same user)
  • Success rate: Sometimes unique amounts fully deanonymize

Graph analysis:

  • Mapping all possible connections between addresses
  • Finding clusters of related activity
  • Success rate: Can identify 20-30% of users with high confidence

Cross-chain analysis:

  • Correlating activity across multiple chains
  • Bridge transaction timing/amounts
  • Success rate: Moderate but improving

Intersection attacks:

  • If you use multiple privacy tools, intersection of anonymity sets can deanonymize
  • Example: Only 5 people used both Tornado and Railgun for same amount = now 1-in-5 instead of 1-in-1,000

Protecting against deanonymization:

  1. Large anonymity sets: Use popular pools with thousands of users
  2. Randomize everything: Amounts, timing, patterns
  3. Wait longer: The longer you wait, the more users join your anonymity set
  4. Split amounts: Never shield and unshield same exact amount
  5. Avoid patterns: Don't use privacy tools on predictable schedule
  6. Cross-chain privacy: Be extra careful when bridging, don't use same amounts
  7. Assume sophisticated adversary: If nation-state is after you, even best privacy tools may not be sufficient

Privacy budget concept:

Each privacy leak reduces your anonymity budget:

  • Unique amount: -50% anonymity
  • Fast timing: -30% anonymity
  • Pattern detection: -40% anonymity
  • Social connection: -80% anonymity (tweeting about private transaction)

Multiplicative effect: Multiple leaks can fully deanonymize even with good tools.

The fundamental limitation:

No privacy tool can protect against all threats. Against motivated nation-state adversary with unlimited resources, determined to identify you, even perfect cryptographic privacy may not be enough (they'll use non-cryptographic methods: social engineering, device compromise, etc.).

Privacy tools work best for:
- Protecting against mass surveillance
- Preventing casual doxing
- Stopping automated chain analysis
- Maintaining privacy from corporations/competitors

They work less well against:
- Targeted nation-state surveillance
- Adversaries with social graph access
- Long-term determined investigation
- Physical device compromise

Know your threat model and use appropriate tools.

responsible_use.title: Responsible Privacy Use
responsible_use.content:
Privacy is a right, but rights come with responsibilities. Using privacy tools ethically and legally protects both you and the broader privacy ecosystem.

Ethical guidelines for privacy tool use:

1. Privacy ≠ Criminality

  • Use privacy for legitimate confidentiality needs
  • Don't use privacy to hide crimes
  • Remember: Privacy protects you, not your illegal actions
  • Analogy: Curtains on your windows are normal, but don't prevent investigation of crimes inside

2. Comply with laws

  • Pay taxes on gains, even from private transactions
  • Report holdings honestly to authorities when required
  • Use viewing keys/disclosure when legally obligated
  • Don't help others evade legitimate legal requirements

3. Consider externalities

  • Your use of privacy tools affects ecosystem perception
  • High-profile criminal use leads to crackdowns on everyone
  • Support privacy tools with compliance features
  • Educate others on legitimate use cases

4. Support good actors

  • Use privacy tools that cooperate with compliance
  • Avoid mixers known for primarily criminal use
  • Support development of compliant privacy solutions
  • Don't fund or promote privacy tools used mainly for crime

Responsible use cases:

✅ Legitimate privacy needs:

  • Protecting salary information from colleagues
  • Hiding donation recipients from public scrutiny
  • Preventing competitors from seeing business operations
  • Protecting families from $5 wrench attacks
  • Maintaining personal financial dignity
  • Protecting dissidents in oppressive regimes
  • Journalist source protection
  • Medical privacy for health-related transactions

❌ Problematic use cases:

  • Hiding proceeds of hacks, thefts, or scams
  • Evading taxes on legitimate gains
  • Money laundering for drug trafficking
  • Terrorism financing
  • Sanctions evasion (unless legitimate humanitarian reasons)
  • Helping others commit crimes

Gray areas (context-dependent):

  • Evading unjust laws in oppressive countries
  • Protecting funds from corrupt authorities
  • Civil disobedience using privacy tools
  • Whistleblower payments

Being a good privacy citizen:

  1. Educate others: Help people understand privacy is normal, not criminal
  2. Use responsibly: Don't give ammunition to privacy opponents
  3. Support good projects: Fund and use privacy tools with compliance features
  4. Advocate politically: Support laws that protect privacy rights
  5. Report bugs responsibly: If you find privacy tool vulnerabilities, disclose responsibly
  6. Contribute to development: Help build better, more compliant privacy solutions

The social contract:

Privacy tools exist in a social context. For them to remain legal and accessible:

  • Users must use them responsibly (not for crime)
  • Developers must include compliance features
  • Regulators must recognize legitimate privacy needs
  • Society must accept privacy as a right, not a privilege

When any group violates this contract (users committing crimes, regulators banning all privacy, developers ignoring compliance), the whole ecosystem suffers.

Your role in privacy's future:

Every time you use privacy tools:

  • You're making a statement about privacy rights
  • You're voting for a future with financial confidentiality
  • You're supporting privacy developers and researchers
  • You're demonstrating legitimate privacy demand

Use that power wisely.

Final thoughts:

Privacy isn't about having something to hide. It's about having something to protect: your dignity, your safety, your autonomy, your right to live without constant surveillance.

In a world where blockchain transparency is the default, privacy tools restore the balance that exists in traditional finance. They're not loopholes or hacks—they're essential infrastructure for a free society.

Use them. Support them. Advocate for them. But also use them responsibly, so they remain available for everyone who needs them.

Privacy is a right. Protect it.

zero_knowledge_proof.definition: A cryptographic method that allows one party to prove to another that a statement is true without revealing any information beyond the validity of the statement itself. In blockchain, ZKPs enable private transactions by proving a transaction is valid without revealing sender, recipient, or amount.

mixer.definition: A service that pools cryptocurrency from multiple users and redistributes it to break the link between sender and recipient addresses. Users deposit funds, which are mixed with other users' funds, then withdraw to fresh addresses. Tornado Cash was the most popular Ethereum mixer before being sanctioned in 2022.

stealth_address.definition: A one-time address generated for receiving payments that only the recipient can access, without observers being able to link it to the recipient's identity or other addresses. Each payment uses a fresh address, preventing transaction history tracking.

ring_signature.definition: A cryptographic signature that proves the signer is one member of a group (the 'ring'), but doesn't reveal which member. Used by Monero to hide transaction senders—observers know one of the ring members sent the transaction, but not which one.

nullifier.definition: A unique cryptographic value that proves a commitment or note has been spent without revealing which specific commitment it was. Nullifiers prevent double-spending in privacy systems while maintaining transaction confidentiality. Used in Zcash, Aztec, and similar zk-SNARK-based protocols.

shielded_transaction.definition: A transaction where sender, recipient, and/or amount are encrypted and hidden from public view, but the transaction's validity is cryptographically proven. Originated with Zcash, now used by various privacy protocols like Railgun and Penumbra.

private_pool.definition: A smart contract or blockchain state that holds encrypted balances and processes private transactions. Users can deposit assets into the pool (shielding), transact privately within it, and withdraw (unshielding). The larger the pool's user base, the stronger the privacy guarantees.

compliance.definition: The ability to prove adherence to regulations while maintaining privacy. Modern privacy tools include compliance features like Private Proof of Innocence (proving funds aren't from sanctioned sources), viewing keys (selective disclosure to auditors), and payment proofs (demonstrating specific transactions occurred).

anonymity_set.definition: The group of users among whom you cannot be distinguished. If 1,000 people used a mixer and you're one of them, your anonymity set is 1,000—observers know you're one of these users but can't determine which. Larger anonymity sets provide stronger privacy.

viewing_key.definition: A cryptographic key that allows read-only access to private transactions and balances without enabling spending. Users can share viewing keys with auditors, tax authorities, or compliance officers to prove transaction details while maintaining privacy from the general public. Different types include full viewing keys (see all transactions), incoming viewing keys (see only received payments), and outgoing viewing keys (see only sent payments).
